section.paragraph: After defining the terms ‘expression’ and ‘equation’ earlier, we have used them throughout this book. We have simplified many kinds of expressions and solved many kinds of equations. We have simplified many rational expressions so far in this chapter. Now we will solve a rational equation.

note.title: Rational Equation
note.paragraph: A rational equation is an equation that contains a rational expression.

section.paragraph: You must make sure to know the difference between rational expressions and rational equations. The equation contains an equal sign.

$$\begin{matrix} \text{Rational Expression} & & & \text{Rational Equation} \\ \begin{matrix} {\frac{1}{8}x + \frac{1}{2}} \\ \frac{y + 6}{y^{2} - 36} \\ {\frac{1}{n - 3} + \frac{1}{n + 4}} \end{matrix} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {\frac{1}{8}x + \frac{1}{2}} & = & \frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{y + 6}{y^{2} - 36} & = & {y + 1} \\ {\frac{1}{n - 3} + \frac{1}{n + 4}} & = & \frac{15}{n^{2} + n - 12} \end{array} \end{matrix}$$
section.heading: Solve Rational Equations
section.paragraph: We have already solved linear equations that contained fractions. We found the LCD of all the fractions in the equation and then multiplied both sides of the equation by the LCD to “clear” the fractions.

We will use the same strategy to solve rational equations. We will multiply both sides of the equation by the LCD. Then, we will have an equation that does not contain rational expressions and thus is much easier for us to solve. But because the original equation may have a variable in a denominator, we must be careful that we don’t end up with a solution that would make a denominator equal to zero.

So before we begin solving a rational equation, we examine it first to find the values that would make any denominators zero. That way, when we solve a rational equation we will know if there are any algebraic solutions we must discard.
An algebraic solution to a rational equation that would cause any of the rational expressions to be undefined is called an extraneous solution to a rational equation.

note.source_type: Extraneous Solution to a Rational Equation
note.title: Extraneous Solution to a Rational Equation
note.paragraph: An extraneous solution to a rational equation is an algebraic solution that would cause any of the expressions in the original equation to be undefined.

section.paragraph: We note any possible extraneous solutions, c, by writing $$x \neq c$$ next to the equation.

example.title: How to Solve a Rational Equation

section.paragraph: The steps of this method are shown.

list.item: Step 1. Note any value of the variable that would make any denominator zero.
Step 2. Find the least common denominator of all denominators in the equation.
Step 3. Clear the fractions by multiplying both sides of the equation by the LCD.
Step 5. Check: If any values found in Step 1 are algebraic solutions, discard them. Check any remaining solutions in the original equation.

section.paragraph: We always start by noting the values that would cause any denominators to be zero.

section.heading: Use Rational Functions
section.paragraph: Working with functions that are defined by rational expressions often lead to rational equations. Again, we use the same techniques to solve them.

problem.paragraph: For rational function, $$f(x) = \frac{2x - 6}{x^{2} - 8x + 15},$$ ⓐ find the domain of the function, ⓑ solve $$f(x) = 1,$$ and ⓒ find the points on the graph at this function value.

solution.paragraph: ⓐ The domain of a rational function is all real numbers except those that make the rational expression undefined. So to find them, we will set the denominator equal to zero and solve.

row.cell: The domain is all real numbers except $$x \neq 3,x \neq 5.$$
Multiply both sides by the LCD, $$\left( {x - 3} \right)\left( {x - 5} \right).$$

solution.paragraph: However, $$x = 3$$ is outside the domain of this function, so we discard that root as extraneous.
ⓒ The value of the function is 1 when $$x = 7.$$ So the points on the graph of this function when $$f(x) = 1$$ is $$\left. \left( {7,1} \right) \right)$$

section.heading: Solve a Rational Equation for a Specific Variable
section.paragraph: When we solved linear equations, we learned how to solve a formula for a specific variable. Many formulas used in business, science, economics, and other fields use rational equations to model the relation between two or more variables. We will now see how to solve a rational equation for a specific variable.
When we developed the point-slope formula from our slope formula, we cleared the fractions by multiplying by the LCD.

$$\begin{array}{cccrll} & & & m & = & \frac{y - y_{1}}{x - x_{1}} \\ { \text{Multiply both sides of the equation by} x - x_{1}.} & & & {m\left( {x - x_{1}} \right)} & = & {\left( \frac{y - y_{1}}{x - x_{1}} \right)\left( {x - x_{1}} \right)} \\ \text{Simplify.} & & & {m\left( {x - x_{1}} \right)} & = & {y - y_{1}} \\ { \text{Rewrite the equation with the} y \text{terms on the left.} } & & & {y - y_{1}} & = & {m\left( {x - x_{1}} \right)} \end{array}$$

In the next example, we will use the same technique with the formula for slope that we used to get the point-slope form of an equation of a line through a point in Chapter 3. We will add one more step to solve for y.

row.cell: Note any value of the variable that wouldmake any denominator zero.
Clear the fractions by multiplying both sides ofthe equation by the LCD, $$x - 3.$$

section.paragraph: Remember to multiply both sides by the LCD in the next example.

row.cell: Note any value of the variable that would makeany denominator zero.
Clear the fractions by multiplying both sides ofthe equations by the LCD, cm.
Collect the terms with c to the right.
Factor the expression on the right.
To isolate c, divide both sides by $$m - 1.$$
Notice that even though we excluded $$c = 0,m = 0$$ from the original equation, we must also now state that $$m \neq 1.$$
